intro: Woolland is a hamlet in Dorset's Blackmore Vale, between Blandford Forum and Sturminster Newton, and south of its small 1855 church stands a great stout yew about 9.5 metres round near the ground. Its girth has barely changed since 1944. The church stands on an early Saxon site, and one yew writer suggested the tree may have sheltered three or four churches. There is no practical public transport, so plan to drive. The churchyard is open and free.
meta_description: Measured at 31 feet 4 inches in 1944 and 31 feet 1 in 2012, the Woolland yew in the Blackmore Vale stands beside an 1855 church on an early Saxon site.
question_meta: Woolland's oldest tree is the stout churchyard yew south of the 1855 church, in the Ancient Yew Group's top class at 9.47 metres round.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Woolland is the yew south of the 1855 church, 947 centimetres round near the ground when Peter Norton measured it in 2012. The Ancient Yew Group places it in its top class of seven metres and over, an estimate from size. Nobody has dated it.
question_context: The Woolland yew has been measured for more than seventy years. In 1944 it was measured at 31 feet 4 inches for Vaughan Cornish's book The Churchyard Yew and Immortality. In 1998 it was 31 feet at one foot up, and in 2012 Peter Norton found 947 centimetres at 30 centimetres, or 31 feet 1. Seventy years, and almost no change. The church beside it was built in 1855 on an early Saxon site. Baxter's book The Eternal Yew, as quoted by the Ancient Yew Group, suggests it may be the only yew to have sheltered three or four churches, a claim from one writer rather than a record. The Group classes yews of seven metres and over as ancient, and that is an estimate from girth, not a date. It was photographed again in 2026. Woolland itself is a small hamlet in the Blackmore Vale with no practical bus, so a car is the realistic way to get here.

faq.q: Where is the yew in Woolland?
faq.a: South of the small church of 1855, in the open churchyard.

faq.q: Has the Woolland yew grown since it was first measured?
faq.a: Barely. It was 31 feet 4 inches in 1944 and 31 feet 1 inch, or 947 centimetres, in 2012.

trees.name: Woolland Yew
trees.story:
The church beside this yew was built in 1855, and the yew may have watched three or four churches come and go before it. That is the suggestion of Baxter's book The Eternal Yew, quoted by the Ancient Yew Group, which calls it possibly the only yew to have sheltered so many. It is one writer's claim, not a record. The ground it rests on is real enough. The present church stands on an early Saxon site in the Blackmore Vale.

The tree itself is a great stout yew south of that church, and it barely changes. In 1944 it was measured for Vaughan Cornish's The Churchyard Yew and Immortality at 31 feet 4 inches. In 1998 it was 31 feet at one foot up. In 2012 Peter Norton found 947 centimetres at 30 centimetres, which is 31 feet 1. Seventy years, three tapes and almost no movement, which tells you a great deal about how slowly an old yew lives.

The Ancient Yew Group puts yews of this girth in its top class, seven metres and over, an estimate from size rather than a dating. It was photographed again in 2026. Woolland is a hamlet with no practical bus, so plan to drive, and give the tree more time than the church.
